picks.explanation: Philadelphia is the better team, nobody's arguing that, but a run and a half is a lot of cushion in a game the sim sees decided by a single crooked inning. Sanchez is genuinely tough on lefties and pretty ordinary against righties, and the Cardinals happen to run a righty-heavy order featuring Herrera, who's been mashing everything with a pulse. Add a warm night with the wind blowing out at a park that already plays like a launching pad, and the "Phillies roll" script gets a lot harder to write cleanly. The model has this covering nearly 60% of the time and the board is selling it at a coin flip, which is the entire reason we're here.

Houston is the better team, nobody's arguing that, but a run and a half is a lot of cushion for a game the simulations keep spitting out as a one-run coin flip. Javier's surface numbers hide a walk problem that turns lineups over for free, and his xwOBA-against sits at a very ordinary .286 that says the whiffs aren't coming to bail him out. Basso is no ace either, but he limits barrels well enough to keep Alvarez from single-handedly running away with this, and a roof-closed game with league-average run scoring is exactly the environment where blowouts don't materialize. Our sim has this landing inside a run more than 65% of the time, and -130 to catch that world is the entire pitch.

Boston is the better team, nobody is arguing that, but a run and a half is a lot of cushion when the Giants have the best bat on the field and the wind is blowing straight in. Devers against right-handed pitching is the kind of profile that ruins tidy blowout scripts, and a .391 xwOBA in that split says the middle of this San Francisco order does not roll over cheaply. The park is playing neutral on runs but suppressing homers tonight, which nudges this toward the grinding, one-swing-decides-it game that run line dogs feast on. Our sim lands on a half-run margin, and the market is pricing something closer to a comfortable Boston win. At -110 you are getting a coin flip on a game that projects tighter than that.

They can, at least often enough to make a near-3-to-1 dog absurd, because Reynolds and Cruz have the barrel profiles that punish exactly the mistakes Snell mixes in when his walk rate creeps toward double digits. Bachar isn't Snell, but the park suppresses runs and the sim has this as a one-run game, not the blowout the board is selling. At +255 you need Pittsburgh to win roughly one in four tries, and the math says closer to one in three. That's the whole ticket.

The Dodgers being nine-figure favorites doesn't mean they win by a truck, and a run and a half is a lot of cushion when Snell is the guy expected to bury an underdog. He walks the ballpark when he isn't missing bats, and Pittsburgh's lefty-mashing bats (Reynolds and Gonzales both post better numbers against southpaws) are set up to make him work through traffic. Bachar isn't good, but this is a homer park playing in Pittsburgh's favor only in the sense that one swing keeps the Pirates within striking distance late. Getting plus money on a one-run loss covering is the entire angle, and +110 pays you to bet against the blowout narrative the board is selling.
